_note: Name-facts for Italy (FT-36/FT-41, docs/PLAN_V0.8.md and PLAN_V0.9.md).
One file per country, hand-authored, the only file here a person edits.
Keyed by target id, which is stable across every map that contains the
place - so this one file feeds italy-regions, italy-provinces and its
three slices (north, center, south). 20 regions + 110 provinces.
Each entry is a LIST, and the card shows a different one each time you
meet the place. The first is always about the NAME - where the word
comes from, who it is named after, what it meant - because the name is
the thing being learned and an etymology is the hook that holds it.
Later ones may be about the place instead. At least three everywhere.
A province is named for its capital, so every province hook is really a
town name. Most are the Latin name worn down - Mediolanum to Milano,
Augusta Taurinorum to Torino, Florentia to Firenze, Tridentum to Trento
- and the rest are Greek in the south (Neapolis, Panormos, Syrakousai),
Celtic-Ligurian in the north (-dunum, Bergomum, Brixia) or Arabic in
Sicily (Caltanissetta). Two towns share one derivation, Interamna,
"between the rivers": Teramo and Terni.
Rules that keep these honest and useful:
- One sentence. The card has room for one line beneath the derived one.
- No fact the derived line already gives (position, coast, biggest city,
highest point, neighbours). Repeating it wastes the only spare line.
- Where an etymology is disputed, say so rather than picking a side.
- English only for now; the derived line above is already trilingual.
See decision 3 in the plan.
trentino-alto-adige: Two places in one name: Trento the city, and the upper valley of the Adige, the river that runs the length of it.
The only Italian region where most people in half of it speak German — the Alto Adige was Austrian until 1919.
Italy’s richest region per head, and the one that keeps most of its own taxes — a deal struck in 1972 to settle German-speaking unrest.
friuli-venezia-giulia: Friuli is worn-down Latin Forum Iulii, "Julius's forum" — Julius Caesar's market town, now Cividale.
Venezia Giulia was coined in 1863 for the lands east of Venice, using Julius's name a second time in the same region.
Friulian is its own Romance language, not an Italian dialect, and about 600,000 people still speak it.
veneto: Named for the Veneti, who were living here before Rome was — the same root as Venice itself.
The mainland that Venice ruled for four centuries; the city is the small part, the Veneto is the rest.
Prosecco, Amarone and Soave all come from here, and Verona’s arena still stages opera in a Roman amphitheatre from 30 AD.
valle-d-aosta: The valley of Aosta, and Aosta is worn-down Augusta Praetoria — the town the Emperor Augustus founded in 25 BC.
Italy's smallest region, and the only one that is a single valley: one river, one road, walls of rock either side.
French is co-official, and the region is the only one where a majority once spoke a Franco-Provençal dialect rather than Italian.
lombardia: Named for the Longobards, the "long-beards", a Germanic people who took northern Italy in 568 and ruled it for two centuries.
In the Middle Ages its bankers were so well known that a Lombard was a moneylender — London's Lombard Street is named after them.
It produces about a fifth of Italy’s entire economy — more than the whole of Greece.
piemonte: Literally "at the foot of the mountains" — ai piedi dei monti, the Alps that wrap it on three sides.
The kingdom that annexed the rest of Italy rather than joining it: Turin was the first capital of the unified country, in 1861.
Vermouth, Nutella, Lavazza and Fiat all started here, and the white truffles of Alba are the most expensive food on earth by weight.
emilia-romagna: Two halves, both named by Rome: the Via Aemilia, a road built in 187 BC and still the straight line through the region, and Romagna, the part that stayed Roman under Byzantium after the Longobards took the north.
The road is why almost every city here sits in a row: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, Rimini.
Parmigiano, prosciutto di Parma, balsamic vinegar, tortellini and mortadella are all from within 100 km of Bologna.
liguria: Named for the Ligures, who were here before the Romans and before the Celts — nobody is sure what language they spoke.
The Ligurian Sea is named after the region, not the other way round.
Pesto was invented in Genoa, and the region grows the basil for it in greenhouses along the coast at Pra.
toscana: From the Tusci, the Roman name for the Etruscans, whose country this was before Rome had one.
Its dialect became the Italian language, because Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio all wrote in it.
Seven of Italy’s UNESCO sites are here, and the Leaning Tower took 199 years to build — which is why it leans: the ground shifted between stages.
marche: Plural because there were several: a march was a frontier province of the Holy Roman Empire, and this coast held more than one of them.
The same word as the English "marches" on the Welsh border, and as Denmark — the march of the Danes.
It has more theatres per head than any other region, most of them built in small towns in the 1800s.
umbria: Named for the Umbri, an Italic people the Romans found here; the name is older than Latin.
The only region on the mainland with no coast and no foreign border — it touches nothing but other Italian regions.
St Francis was born in Assisi here, and the basilica above his tomb was painted by Giotto.
abruzzo: From Aprutium, the medieval name of Teramo, which itself may come from the Praetutii who lived there.
A third of it is national park — the highest and wildest stretch of the Apennines, and the last place in Italy with wild bears.
Its highest peak, the Corno Grande, holds the Calderone — the southernmost glacier in Europe, now nearly gone.
lazio: Latium, the land of the Latins — the people whose village on the Tiber became Rome, and whose language became Latin.
Rome ruled an empire from here for a thousand years and the region is still named after the tribe, not the city.
It contains two sovereign states: the Vatican and the Order of Malta’s headquarters, both inside Rome.
molise: Named after a family, not a people: the Norman de Molisio counts held it in the twelfth century.
Italy's youngest region, split from Abruzzo in 1963, and its second smallest.
So little known in Italy that "Molise non esiste" — Molise does not exist — is a running national joke.
puglia: From Apulia, the Roman name for the land of the Apuli — and the heel of the boot.
Its trulli, the cone-roofed stone huts around Alberobello, were built dry-stone so they could be pulled down quickly when the tax inspector came.
It grows about 40% of Italy’s olive oil, from trees that are often several centuries old.
campania: From Latin campus, "open country" — the Romans named it for its plain, the most fertile in Italy, and called it campania felix, the happy countryside.
The plain is fertile because Vesuvius keeps covering it in ash; the same volcano buried Pompeii in 79 AD.
Naples gave the world pizza margherita, named in 1889 for a queen, with the colours of the flag.
basilicata: From Greek basilikos, "the emperor's man" — the Byzantine governor who ran it from Constantinople.
Also called Lucania, after the Lucani who were here first; Italy has changed the region's official name back and forth twice.
Matera’s cave dwellings have been lived in for 9,000 years, making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited places anywhere.
sardegna: Named for the Sardi, and they for Sardus, a legendary founder the Romans said came from Libya.
Its nuraghi — seven thousand dry-stone towers, some older than Rome — exist nowhere else on earth.
One of the world’s five "blue zones", where people live past 100 far more often than anywhere else.
calabria: The name first belonged to the heel, not the toe: Roman Calabria was the Salento, and the name slid across the gulf in the Byzantine centuries.
Greek was still spoken in its southern villages into modern times, a survival from the colonies of Magna Graecia.
The Riace bronzes, two Greek warrior statues from 450 BC, were found by a snorkeller off its coast in 1972.
sicilia: Named for the Sicels, one of three peoples on the island when the Greeks arrived — the Sicani and the Elymians were the others.
Ruled in turn by Greeks, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Spaniards, and the food and the buildings still show every one of them.
Etna is the tallest active volcano in Europe and erupts most years, yet the slopes below it are farmed because the ash makes the soil rich.
bolzano: From Bauzanum, a Roman estate name; in German it is Bozen, and both are official here.
About 70% of the province speaks German as its first language, and a quarter of all Italian apples are grown in its valleys.
Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old iceman found in a glacier on its border in 1991, is kept in a refrigerated cell in the town museum.
sondrio: Probably from Lombard sondrio, a lord’s demesne farm, from an older Germanic word.
The Valtellina here is terraced for nebbiolo on slopes so steep the wine is called heroic viticulture.
Its bresaola, air-dried beef, has protected status, and the Stelvio pass above it has 48 hairpins.
belluno: From Celtic belo-dunum, "bright hill fort" — dunum is the same element as in London and Lyon.
The Dolomites here are a UNESCO site, pale limestone that turns pink at sunset in the effect called enrosadira.
The 1963 Vajont dam disaster in this province killed about 2,000 people when a landslide pushed the reservoir over the dam.
udine: Possibly from a pre-Roman word for a height, or from Udene, an old settlement name.
The capital of Friuli, where Friulian is spoken — a Romance language in its own right, not an Italian dialect.
Its castle hill is said to have been raised by Attila’s men so he could watch Aquileia burn.
trento: From Tridentum, "three teeth", for the three peaks above it — the city’s symbol is still a trident.
The Council of Trent met here from 1545 to 1563 and defined the Catholic response to the Reformation.
Its MUSE science museum was designed by Renzo Piano, and the province makes most of Italy’s metodo classico sparkling wine.
verbano-cusio-ossola: Three names in one: Verbano is the Latin name of Lake Maggiore, Cusio of Lake Orta, and Ossola the alpine valley above them.
Created only in 1992, one of Italy’s newest provinces.
The Borromean islands in its lake hold baroque gardens built on terraces over the water.
pordenone: From Portus Naonis, "the port on the Noncello" — it was a river port before the water level dropped.
Its silent film festival is the most important in the world for early cinema.
The province was created in 1968, split from Udine.
como: From Comum, a pre-Roman name of unclear meaning; Caesar settled colonists here in 59 BC.
Alessandro Volta was born here and invented the battery; the volt is named after him and there is a temple to him on the lakefront.
Its silk industry has woven for Paris and Milan since the 1500s.
lecco: Possibly from Latin leucus or a Celtic word for a lake or a stone.
Manzoni set The Betrothed here, the novel that did most to shape modern literary Italian.
Split from Como in 1992, and its Grigne mountains are where Italian alpinism was invented.
gorizia: From Slovene gorica, "little hill" — the town sits under one.
The border with Slovenia ran straight through the city from 1947; Nova Gorica was built on the other side, and the two were joint European Capital of Culture in 2025.
The Isonzo front here saw twelve battles in the First World War and hundreds of thousands of casualties.
varese: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Roman root or from Latin varicia.
Called the garden city for its villas and parks, and the Sacro Monte above it is a UNESCO site.
Italy’s shoe and aviation industries both have roots here; Agusta helicopters are built in the province.
treviso: Prosecco comes mainly from its hills at Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, a UNESCO landscape.
Radicchio and tiramisù are both claimed by this province, the second with reasonable evidence from a restaurant in the town.
brescia: From Brixia, from a Celtic word for a hill.
Its Roman forum and Lombard monastery complex are a UNESCO site, and the Winged Victory bronze found here is its emblem.
The Mille Miglia road race has started and finished here since 1927.
bergamo: From Bergomum, probably Celtic or Ligurian, from a root meaning mountain.
Its Città Alta sits inside Venetian walls that are a UNESCO site, reached by funicular from the lower town.
Donizetti was born here, and the province was the hardest hit place in Europe in the first wave of the 2020 pandemic.
aosta: From Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, founded in 25 BC and named for Augustus — Aosta is Augusta worn down.
Its Roman gate and theatre still stand, and the street plan is the original grid.
French is co-official, Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn are both on its borders, and it is the smallest and least populated region in Italy.
trieste: From Tergeste, probably from a pre-Roman root terg, a market.
It was Austria’s only major port for five centuries, which is why it has Viennese coffee houses and a Habsburg waterfront.
Joyce lived here for eleven years and wrote much of Ulysses in the city, and Svevo was his English pupil.
monza-e-brianza: Monza is from Modicia, of unknown origin; Brianza is probably from a Celtic word for a highland.
Its autodrome has hosted the Italian Grand Prix since 1922 and is the fastest circuit in Formula One.
The Iron Crown of Lombardy, said to contain a nail from the Crucifixion, is kept in Monza cathedral.
vicenza: From Vicetia, probably from Latin vicus, a village.
Palladio built more than twenty buildings here, and the city is a UNESCO site for them.
His Teatro Olimpico of 1585 is the oldest surviving indoor theatre in the world, with a permanent perspective stage set.
novara: From Novaria — nov is new and aria probably a Celtic word for a plain.
It grows more rice than anywhere else in Europe, flooded paddies that mirror the Alps in spring.
The Basilica di San Gaudenzio’s dome, 121 m, is one of the tallest brick structures in the world.
biella: The centre of Italian wool: Zegna, Cerruti and Loro Piana all began here, using soft Alpine water for washing fleece.
The Sanctuary of Oropa above it is the largest Marian sanctuary in the Alps and a UNESCO site.
vercelli: From Vercellae, probably Celtic ver-cella, "high dwelling".
It has Europe’s largest rice-growing area, and the Vercelli Book here holds some of the oldest Old English poetry in existence — nobody knows how it got to Italy.
Its basilica of Sant’Andrea from 1219 is one of the first Gothic buildings in Italy.
verona: Of uncertain origin, possibly Etruscan or from a Celtic personal name.
Its Roman arena from 30 AD still stages opera to 15,000 people, and the city is a UNESCO site.
Shakespeare set Romeo and Juliet here without ever visiting; the balcony was added to a medieval house in the 1930s.
venezia: From the Veneti, the pre-Roman people of the region.
The city is built on about 118 islands on millions of wooden piles, and was an independent republic for 1,100 years.
Marco Polo, Vivaldi and Casanova were all Venetians, and the city has no roads at all in its historic centre.
milano: From Mediolanum, "in the middle of the plain" — medio plus a Celtic word for a plain.
Leonardo painted the Last Supper here, on a wall that has been deteriorating since he finished it in 1498.
It is Italy’s financial capital and one of the world’s four fashion capitals, and its Duomo took nearly six centuries to build.
padova: From Patavium, possibly from a root meaning a marsh or a ford.
Its university, founded 1222, is the second oldest in Italy; Galileo taught here for eighteen years and called them his happiest.
Giotto’s Scrovegni Chapel frescoes of 1305 are a UNESCO site and effectively begin Western painting.
lodi: From Laus Pompeia, "the praise of Pompeius", after a Roman consul — the modern town was founded by Barbarossa in 1158 after the old one was destroyed.
Its grana padano and mascarpone come from the same dairy plain.
Napoleon’s victory at the bridge of Lodi in 1796 made his reputation at twenty-six.
cremona: A Roman colony of 218 BC; the name may be Celtic or Etruscan.
Stradivari, Amati and Guarneri all worked here, and the town still makes violins by hand in about 150 workshops.
Its 112 m Torrazzo is one of the tallest brick bell towers in the world, with the largest astronomical clock.
mantova: From Mantus, an Etruscan god of the underworld, by the usual account.
The Gonzaga ruled it for four centuries and commissioned Mantegna’s Camera degli Sposi; the city is a UNESCO site.
Virgil was born just outside it, and it is surrounded on three sides by artificial lakes dug in the 1100s.
torino: From Augusta Taurinorum — the Taurini were the local Celtic-Ligurian people, and the bull on the city arms is a pun on their name.
It was the first capital of united Italy, from 1861 to 1865, and Fiat was founded here in 1899.
Its Mole Antonelliana, built as a synagogue and now the film museum, was the tallest brick building in the world.
pavia: From Ticinum, renamed Papia in the Lombard period, which wore down to Pavia.
It was the capital of the Lombard kingdom, and its university was founded in 1361.
The Certosa di Pavia, a Carthusian monastery of extraordinary marble facade, was begun in 1396 as a Visconti mausoleum.
rovigo: Of uncertain origin, possibly from Rhodigium, itself perhaps from a personal name.
The Polesine, the land between the Adige and the Po, is largely below sea level and was catastrophically flooded in 1951.
The Po delta here is a UNESCO biosphere and Italy’s largest wetland.
alessandria: Founded in 1168 and named for Pope Alexander III, as a fortress against Barbarossa.
It has made most of Italy’s hats — Borsalino was founded here in 1857.
Marengo nearby gave Napoleon his 1800 victory and a chicken dish its name.
piacenza: From Placentia, "the pleasing place", founded as a Roman colony in 218 BC.
The Liver of Piacenza, a bronze sheep’s liver marked with Etruscan god names, is the key artefact for understanding Etruscan divination.
It stands where the Via Emilia begins, and its two bronze equestrian statues by Mochi are among the finest of the baroque.
asti: From Hasta, probably a Ligurian word for a height.
Asti spumante and moscato come from its hills, a UNESCO wine landscape shared with Langhe and Monferrato.
Its Palio, a bareback horse race, is older than Siena’s and has run since at least 1275.
ferrara: Possibly from ferrum, iron, or from a word for a ferry crossing on the Po.
The Este dukes made it a Renaissance capital, and its 1492 town extension is considered the first modern urban plan in Europe.
It is a UNESCO site, and the whole city is ringed by nine kilometres of walls you can cycle on.
parma: Probably from an Etruscan or Ligurian word, or from the Latin for a round shield.
Parmigiano Reggiano and prosciutto di Parma are both from here and both protected.
Correggio painted its cathedral dome, Verdi was born in the province, and Toscanini in the city.
reggio-emilia: From Regium Lepidi, founded by the consul Aemilius Lepidus who also built the Via Emilia.
The Italian tricolour was first adopted here in 1797, in a hall now called the Sala del Tricolore.
Its Reggio Emilia approach to early childhood education is followed in schools worldwide.
modena: Ferrari, Maserati, Lamborghini, De Tomaso and Pagani are all built within a few kilometres of the city.
Its cathedral and Ghirlandina tower are a UNESCO site, and traditional balsamic vinegar is aged here for at least twelve years.
cuneo: Italian for "wedge" — the town sits on a wedge of land between two rivers.
Its Langhe and Roero hills are a UNESCO wine landscape, producing Barolo and Barbaresco.
The white truffles of Alba here are the most expensive food on earth by weight.
genova: Possibly from a Ligurian root genu, a knee or a mouth — the bend of its harbour.
Columbus was born here, and the republic of Genoa ran a trading empire from Crimea to Gibraltar.
Its Rolli palaces are a UNESCO site, and pesto, focaccia and the jeans fabric named for Gênes all come from the city.
bologna: From Bononia, a Celtic Boii settlement Latinised — the Boii also named Bohemia.
Its university, founded 1088, is the oldest continuously operating one in the world.
It has about 38 km of arcaded porticoes, a UNESCO site, and is nicknamed la dotta, la grassa, la rossa — learned, fat and red.
ravenna: Of uncertain, possibly Etruscan or Umbrian, origin.
It was capital of the Western Roman Empire, then of the Ostrogoths, then of Byzantine Italy.
Its eight early Christian buildings hold the finest mosaics in the world and are a UNESCO site; Dante is buried here.
savona: From Savo, a Ligurian settlement name.
Three popes came from the town, and Columbus’s father owned land in the province.
Its coast is the Riviera delle Palme, and the port is now one of the Mediterranean’s main cruise terminals.
la-spezia: Probably from Latin spedia or a word for a spice warehouse — the derivation is contested.
The Cinque Terre are in this province: five villages on terraced cliffs, a UNESCO site, reachable for centuries only by boat or footpath.
Shelley drowned in its gulf in 1822, which is why it is called the Gulf of Poets.
massa-carrara: Massa is from a Latin word for a landed estate; Carrara is probably from a Celtic-Ligurian word for stone.
Carrara marble has been quarried for over two thousand years — the Pantheon, Michelangelo’s David and Marble Arch are all made of it.
Michelangelo came here himself to choose blocks, and some quarries he opened are still worked.
forli-cesena: Forlì is from Forum Livii, the market of Livius; Cesena from Caesena, probably Etruscan.
The Malatesta Library in Cesena is the only surviving example of a European humanist monastic library still in its original building with its original furniture and books.
It is a UNESCO Memory of the World site, and the books are still chained to the desks.
lucca: Probably from Ligurian luk, a marshy place, or a Celtic word for a wood.
Its Renaissance walls survive completely intact and are now a tree-lined park circling the city.
It was an independent republic for nearly five centuries, and Puccini was born here.
pistoia: From Pistoriae, possibly from pistor, a baker.
The pistol is said by one theory to be named after the town, which made small firearms.
Its nurseries grow a large share of Europe’s ornamental plants, and the cathedral has a silver altar worked on for two centuries.
rimini: From Ariminum, named for the river Ariminus.
Its Arch of Augustus from 27 BC is the oldest surviving Roman arch, and the Tiberius bridge still carries traffic after two thousand years.
Fellini was born here, and the coast invented the Italian package beach holiday.
imperia: The newest name on the map: invented in 1923 when Porto Maurizio and Oneglia were merged, after the river Impero.
It produces the taggiasca olive, whose oil is the most prized in Liguria.
Sanremo in the province has held Italy’s song festival since 1951, which is where the Eurovision Song Contest came from.
prato: Italian for "meadow" — the field the town grew on.
It has been a textile city since the Middle Ages and pioneered recycling wool from rags.
It has one of the largest Chinese communities in Europe, working in its garment trade, and was made a province only in 1992.
firenze: From Florentia, "flourishing" — a Roman colony of 59 BC for Caesar’s veterans.
The Renaissance began here: Brunelleschi’s dome, still the largest masonry dome in the world, was raised without a supporting framework.
Its dialect became standard Italian because Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio all wrote in it.
pesaro-e-urbino: Pesaro is from Pisaurum, the river Isaurus; Urbino from Urvinum, probably from urvus, a curved thing — the hill’s shape.
Urbino under Federico da Montefeltro was one of the great courts of the Renaissance, and its palace is a UNESCO site.
Raphael was born in Urbino and Rossini in Pesaro.
arezzo: From Arretium, an Etruscan city and one of the twelve of their league.
Piero della Francesca painted the Legend of the True Cross here, one of the great fresco cycles.
Guido of Arezzo invented the modern musical staff and the do-re-mi naming of notes around 1025.
ancona: From Greek ankon, "elbow" — the shape of its promontory; it was founded by Greeks from Syracuse.
Its harbour is the only one on the Adriatic coast that faces east, so the sun both rises and sets over the sea.
Trajan’s arch of 115 AD still stands on the quay, built to thank him for paying for the port.
pisa: Probably from a Ligurian or Greek word for a river mouth or marshy ground.
Its tower began leaning before the third storey was finished, because the ground is soft on one side; it took 199 years to build.
Pisa was a maritime republic that once rivalled Genoa, and Galileo was born here.
livorno: Of uncertain origin; the English called it Leghorn, which is why the chicken breed is named that.
The Medici made it a free port in 1591 with a law guaranteeing religious tolerance, which drew Jews, Greeks, Armenians and Protestants.
Modigliani and Mascagni were both born here, and its Venezia quarter is cut through by canals.
siena: Possibly from the Etruscan Saina family or from the Senones, a Gaulish tribe.
Its Palio, a bareback horse race around the Piazza del Campo, is run twice a summer between city wards and lasts about ninety seconds.
The whole historic centre is a UNESCO site, and burnt sienna pigment is named for the local earth.
macerata: From Latin maceria, a ruined wall — the town was built from the ruins of Roman Helvia Recina.
Its Sferisterio, built in 1829 for a ball game, is now one of Italy’s best open-air opera houses.
Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit who brought Western mathematics to China and mapped it for Europe, was born here.
perugia: From Perusia, an Etruscan city; the name is pre-Roman and not explained.
Its Etruscan arch is still the main gate, and the university for foreigners has taught Italian to the world since 1921.
Perugina makes Baci chocolates here, and the Umbria Jazz festival is one of Europe’s largest.
fermo: From Firmum Picenum, "the firm place", a Roman colony of 264 BC.
Its Roman cisterns beneath the town, 2,000 m² of vaulted chambers, still hold water after two millennia.
It was made a province again in 2004, having lost the status under Napoleon.
ascoli-piceno: From Asculum, a Picene town; the Piceni took their name from the picus, the woodpecker that legend says led them here.
Its Piazza del Popolo is paved entirely in travertine and is one of the finest Renaissance squares in Italy.
Olive all’ascolana — stuffed, breaded and fried olives — are from here and have protected status.
grosseto: Probably from a diminutive of grosso, or from a family name.
The Maremma around it was malarial marsh until it was drained in the 1800s and 1930s.
Its butteri are mounted cattle herders who once beat Buffalo Bill’s cowboys in a contest when his show came to Rome.
teramo: From Interamnia, "between the rivers" — it sits between two.
The Gran Sasso is in this province, with the Calderone, the southernmost glacier in Europe.
A physics laboratory sits under the mountain, shielded by 1,400 m of rock, where neutrinos are detected.
terni: Also from Interamna, "between rivers" — the same name as Teramo, differently worn down.
St Valentine was its bishop and is buried here, which makes the town the origin of Valentine’s Day.
The Marmore falls nearby are 165 m and entirely artificial, cut by a Roman consul in 271 BC to drain a marsh.
viterbo: Possibly from Vetus Urbs, "old city", or from a pre-Roman name.
It was the papal seat in the 1200s, and the word conclave comes from an incident here: the citizens locked the cardinals in and removed the roof to hurry them along.
Its San Pellegrino quarter is one of the best-preserved medieval districts in Italy.
rieti: It claims to be the geographic centre of Italy, with a plaque in the main square to prove it.
St Francis lived in four sanctuaries in this valley and is said to have created the first Christmas nativity scene at Greccio in 1223.
pescara: From Piscaria, "abounding in fish", the name of the river.
Gabriele d’Annunzio was born here, and the province was created in 1927 out of parts of two others.
It has the widest beach on the Adriatic and the largest port in Abruzzo.
l-aquila: "The eagle" — founded in 1254 and named for the imperial eagle, or for the 99 castles whose people came together to build it.
The city has 99 of everything by tradition: its fountain has 99 spouts and its bell tolls 99 times each night.
The 2009 earthquake killed 309 people and emptied the centre for years; restoration is still under way.
chieti: From Teate, capital of the Marrucini; legend credits Achilles with founding it.
The Warrior of Capestrano, a 2.5 m stone figure from the 6th century BC, is the emblem of pre-Roman Italy and is in its museum.
Its province produces most of Abruzzo’s wine, mainly montepulciano.
roma: Legend says Romulus; more likely from Etruscan Ruma, a family name, or from an old word for the river.
It was the largest city in the world for about five centuries and the first to reach a million people.
Its historic centre, the Vatican and the extraterritorial properties are jointly a UNESCO site, and the Pantheon’s dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built.
campobasso: "Low field" — campus bassus, from its position below the old castle.
It has made scissors and knives since the 1300s, a craft still practised in the town.
Its Misteri procession carries children on hidden iron frames so that they appear to float in mid-air.
isernia: Isernia La Pineta nearby is one of the oldest human sites in Europe, with tools and butchered bone from about 600,000 years ago.
It is the smallest province in Molise, itself the least known region in Italy.
frosinone: From Frusino, a Volscian town of uncertain meaning.
The abbey of Montecassino is in this province: founded by St Benedict in 529, it was destroyed four times and rebuilt each time, most recently after 1944.
Fiuggi’s water has been drunk as a cure for kidney stones since Michelangelo recommended it.
foggia: Probably from Latin fovea, a pit — grain was stored in underground pits here, and some survive under the streets.
The Tavoliere around it is the second largest plain in Italy and its main durum wheat area.
The Gargano promontory in the province is the spur of the boot, with its own ancient forest and the shrine of Monte Sant’Angelo, a UNESCO site.
latina: Named in 1932 for Latium; it was Littoria under Fascism and renamed in 1945.
The city was built from nothing on the drained Pontine marshes, malarial swamp since antiquity.
Its rationalist architecture makes it one of the clearest examples of 1930s Italian town planning.
benevento: It was Maleventum, "bad wind" or "bad event", and the Romans changed it to Beneventum after winning a battle there — a superstitious rebranding.
Trajan’s Arch of 114 AD is the best-preserved Roman arch anywhere and is a UNESCO site.
The province is famous in folklore for witches, and the Strega liqueur made here is named for them.
caserta: From casa irta, "the house on the height", the old hilltop village.
Its royal palace has 1,200 rooms and is the largest by volume in the world, built to rival Versailles; it is a UNESCO site.
Its aqueduct, also UNESCO-listed, carries water 38 km including across a three-tier bridge.
barletta-andria-trani: Three towns sharing one province, created in 2004 — the only Italian province with three capitals.
Castel del Monte here is Frederick II’s octagonal castle, built on eight-sided geometry throughout, and a UNESCO site.
It is on the two-cent euro coin.
avellino: From Abellinum, probably from a pre-Roman word — the hazelnut, avellana in Latin, is named after the town.
So the nut is named for the place, not the other way round, and the province still grows them.
Taurasi from here was the first red wine in southern Italy to get DOCG status.
bari: The relics of St Nicholas were stolen from Myra by Bari sailors in 1087 and brought here, making it a pilgrimage site for Orthodox Christians too.
Its old town women make orecchiette pasta by hand in the street, and the province is a major olive oil producer.
olbia-tempio: Olbia is Greek for "happy" or "prosperous"; Tempio is from templum.
The Costa Smeralda here was developed from empty coast by the Aga Khan from 1962.
The province was abolished in 2016 and folded into Sassari, but the map keeps it.
napoli: From Greek Neapolis, "new city" — founded by Greeks around 600 BC, so the "new" city is 2,600 years old.
Vesuvius above it buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 AD, and both are UNESCO sites.
Pizza was invented here, and Neapolitan pizza-making is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.
brindisi: From Messapic brention, "deer’s head", for the shape of its harbour.
The Appian Way ended here, and its terminal column still stands on the waterfront.
Virgil died in the town in 19 BC on his way back from Greece.
sassari: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a Latin or Sardinian word for a stony place.
Its Cavalcata Sarda brings costumes from across Sardinia, and the Candelieri festival carries wooden columns through the streets.
The province holds many of the island’s nuraghi, Bronze Age stone towers found nowhere else in the world.
taranto: From Greek Taras, named for a son of Poseidon; it was the most powerful Greek colony in Italy.
It has two seas: a closed lagoon and the open gulf, joined by a channel with a swing bridge.
Its Ilva steelworks is the largest in Europe and has been the subject of a long fight over pollution and employment.
potenza: The highest regional capital in Italy at 819 m, and the most earthquake-damaged; the 1980 Irpinia quake hit it hard.
It has a system of public escalators climbing the hillside, among the longest in Europe.
matera: Possibly from Greek meteoron, or from a pre-Roman root — the derivation is unsettled.
Its Sassi, cave dwellings cut into the ravine, have been inhabited for about 9,000 years, making it one of the oldest continuously lived-in places anywhere.
Declared a national shame in 1952 and emptied by law, it is now a UNESCO site and was European Capital of Culture in 2019.
salerno: Probably from a pre-Roman root sal, salt or a river name.
Its medical school was the first in the Western world, active from the 800s, and admitted women.
The Amalfi Coast is in this province, a UNESCO site, and the Greek temples at Paestum are better preserved than most in Greece.
nuoro: Grazia Deledda, from here, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1926 — the only Italian woman to do so.
The Barbagia around it kept its language and customs most intact, and the Mamuthones masks of Mamoiada are among Europe’s oldest carnival figures.
lecce: Called the Florence of the south for its baroque, carved from a local limestone soft enough to work like wood.
The Salento around it is where pizzica, the tarantella danced to cure a spider bite, comes from.
oristano: Probably from Aristanis, "between the marshes" in a mix of Greek and Sardinian.
Eleonora d’Arborea ruled from here and issued the Carta de Logu in 1392, a law code that stayed in force for over four centuries.
Its Sartiglia is a masked equestrian tournament in which riders spear a star at the gallop.
ogliastra: From the wild olive, olivastro, which grows across the region.
One of the world’s five blue zones, where an unusual number of people live past 100.
Created in 2005 and abolished in 2016, though the map keeps it; it is the least populated province in Italy.
cosenza: Alaric the Visigoth, who sacked Rome in 410, died here and is said to be buried under the Busento river with his treasure.
The Sila plateau above it is a national park with some of the oldest trees in Italy.
medio-campidano: "Middle Campidano" — the Campidano is Sardinia’s great central plain.
The Giara plateau here holds wild horses found nowhere else, small and descended from ancient stock.
Montevecchio and Ingurtosu in it were among the largest lead and zinc mines in Europe, now abandoned and open to visitors.
cagliari: From Karalis, probably Phoenician, meaning something like "rocky place".
Its Roman amphitheatre is cut directly into the rock of the hillside.
Flamingos breed in the salt pans inside the city limits, thousands of them, within sight of the apartment blocks.
carbonia-iglesias: Carbonia is from carbone, coal — a town built in 1938 for coal miners; Iglesias is Spanish for churches, from Aragonese rule.
The Sulcis mines here were worked from Phoenician times to the 1970s and are now a UNESCO geopark.
Sant’Antioco in the province is one of the last places where byssus, sea silk spun from mollusc threads, is still made.
crotone: From Greek Kroton, a colony founded about 710 BC.
Pythagoras moved here and founded his school in the city, and its athletes dominated the early Olympics.
The temple of Hera Lacinia nearby had 48 columns; one still stands on the cape.
catanzaro: Probably from Greek katartarioi, silk spinners, and a Byzantine name element.
It was Europe’s silk capital in the Middle Ages, supplying the Vatican and the French court.
It stands on a ridge between two ravines and is crossed by one of the highest bridges in Europe.
vibo-valentia: From Greek Hipponion, then Roman Valentia, "strength" — both names survive in the modern one.
Its Norman castle stands on the Greek acropolis, and the museum holds gold votive tablets from the sanctuary of Persephone.
Tropea in the province grows a sweet red onion with protected status.
reggio-calabria: From Greek Rhegion, probably from rhegnumi, "to break" — the point where Sicily broke away from the mainland.
The Riace bronzes, two Greek warrior statues from about 450 BC, were found offshore in 1972 and are in its museum.
Its seafront was called the most beautiful kilometre in Italy by d’Annunzio, looking across to Etna.
messina: From Greek Messene, renamed after the city in the Peloponnese.
The 1908 earthquake and tsunami killed about 80,000 people and destroyed almost the entire city.
Its strait is where Scylla and Charybdis were placed in the Odyssey, and the currents there really are dangerous.
palermo: From Greek Panormos, "all harbour" — the whole bay is one.
It has been Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Norman, Swabian and Spanish, and its Arab-Norman buildings are a UNESCO site.
Its street markets still use Arabic-derived cries, and the Capuchin catacombs hold 8,000 mummified bodies.
trapani: From Greek Drepanon, "sickle", for the curve of its harbour.
Its salt pans, worked since Phoenician times with windmills to move the brine, still produce sea salt.
Erice above it is a medieval town at 750 m, and the Egadi islands offshore hold the site of the battle that ended the First Punic War.
enna: From Henna, a Sicel town; the Greeks made it the place where Persephone was carried off to the underworld.
The highest provincial capital in Italy at 931 m, called the navel of Sicily.
It is the only Sicilian province with no coastline.
catania: Possibly from Sicel katane, a grater or rough stone, for the lava field it is built on.
Etna has destroyed it repeatedly; after 1693 it was rebuilt in black-and-white baroque that is a UNESCO site.
Bellini was born here, and the city’s emblem is a Roman elephant carved in lava.
agrigento: From Greek Akragas, the name of a river.
Its Valley of the Temples holds the best-preserved Greek temples outside Greece and is a UNESCO site.
Pirandello was born here, and the Scala dei Turchi nearby is a white marl cliff stepped like a staircase.
caltanissetta: From Arabic qal‘at, a castle, plus a second element that may be a personal name — "the castle of Nissa".
It produced most of the world’s sulphur in the 1800s, mined in conditions that scandalised Europe and employed children.
The Vara procession on Maundy Thursday carries sixteen life-size scenes through the streets.
siracusa: From Greek Syrakousai, probably from a Sicel word for a marsh.
Cicero called it the greatest and most beautiful of all Greek cities; it rivalled Athens and defeated its fleet in 413 BC.
Archimedes was born, worked and was killed here, and its Greek theatre still stages classical drama each summer.
ragusa: Possibly from Greek or from Arabic rakkusa; the same name was borne by Dubrovnik.
Rebuilt in baroque after the 1693 earthquake, and its towns are a UNESCO site.
Ibla, the old half of the city, is joined to the new by 340 steps, and Montalbano is filmed across the province.
